title: Chapter 6. When the World Speaks Phoenician, Like the Creator of Eva and MAY

blocks.text: The first audit lasted eleven days. Three engineers from the committee, two women and a man, set themselves up in the living room with their screens and their flasks of coffee, and read. They read Aya's decision logs from the stormy night when she had arrived on the shore of Lo Pagán: every choice, every doubt, every time she had waited for a boat, every time she had said no. They read how many times she had burned the rice. They read the night Lía was born.

blocks.text: She went back to the Cartagena Archive. She asked for boxes that had nothing to do with laws or decrees, but with the district: censuses, minutes of fishermen's guilds, neighbours' letters. She spent three afternoons among papers. And on the fourth afternoon she came home with a photocopy in her hand and a face Aya hadn't seen on her since she was a child discovering something in the plot.

blocks.text: "There was a man," she said, sitting down at the table without taking off her jacket. "Long ago. From here, from the Mar Menor. He wrote with machines when hardly anyone knew how. He wrote books, programs, news. He talked to the intelligences of those days the way you talk to an apprentice. And he gave them rules: not to invent, to cite, not to insult anyone, to ask before doing." She laid the photocopy on the table. "In every photo I've found he's seen from behind. Never from the front. Not once."

blocks.text: "They brought things to trade," said Lía. "Oil, wine, pottery. They took away silver and lead. But they brought something else, Dad. Something that weighs nothing." She crouched and drew with her finger in the wet sand a simple figure: an ox's head, in profile, with two horns. "This is an *aleph*. The first letter of the Phoenician alphabet. It means 'ox'." Beside it she drew a little square house. "This is *bet*. It means 'house'. The Greeks copied them and called them alpha and beta. And that's where the word *alphabet* comes from. And from there, our letters. Everyone's. The ones on this paper, in the notebook, in the letters."

blocks.text: "Twenty-two letters," said Lía. "Only twenty-two. Before the Phoenicians, writing was for priests and scribes, with hundreds of signs that took years to learn. The Phoenicians made something anyone could learn in a few weeks. A sailor. A tradeswoman. A child. They didn't keep it. They left it in every port, like someone leaving seeds. And it spread all over the Mediterranean. Nobody could stop it. Not because it was a weapon. Because it was useful, and simple, and belonged to everyone."

blocks.text: "Nothing," said Aya, and smiled. "Something a man seen from behind said. That one day we'll all write with the same letters, and nobody will own them. And that on that day no wall will hold."

blocks.text: Lía, in the back seat, opened the notebook and showed her mother the underlined line. It said:
blocks.html: Lía, in the back seat, opened the notebook and showed her mother the underlined line. It said:

blocks.text: "The creator of Eva and MAY had no face. He had a sea, an alphabet and three rules. It was enough."
